title: Diffusion Models & Generative AI
summary: The generative technique behind modern text-to-image systems — the other half of "Generative AI" beyond LLMs.

slides.markdown:
"Generative AI" isn't only LLMs — the images, audio, and video generated by tools like Stable Diffusion or Midjourney come from a different family: **diffusion models**, which learn to reverse a process of gradually destroying an image with noise.

- Train by **adding noise** to real images step by step, and teaching a model to **predict and remove it**.
- Generate by starting from **pure noise** and running that removal process backward.
- Modern text-to-image systems condition this process on a text description.

slides.subTitle: The generative AI landscape at a glance
slides.markdown:
"Generative AI" spans several distinct model families, each dominant in a different modality: **LLMs** (decoder-only Transformers) for text, **diffusion models** for images and increasingly audio/video, and older families like **GANs** and **VAEs** ([Autoencoders & Generative Basics](autoencoders-generative-basics)) that diffusion has largely displaced for image quality.

The common thread across all of them: learn a distribution over realistic data, then sample new, novel examples from it — the differences are entirely in *how* each family learns and samples that distribution.

slides.subTitle: Adding noise, then learning to reverse it
slides.markdown:
Training works backward from generation: take a real image and add a little Gaussian noise, repeat for hundreds or thousands of steps until it's pure static — the fixed, mathematically-defined **forward (noising) process**, which needs no learning at all.

The model's job is the **reverse**: given a noisy image at step `t`, predict the noise added, so it can be subtracted to get a slightly-less-noisy image at `t-1`. Trained across many images and steps, it learns to turn any noisy image back into something realistic.

slides.subTitle: Forward vs reverse diffusion
slides.markdown:
The two directions of the same process, at training time and generation time:

![Forward (noising) vs reverse (denoising) diffusion](assets/diffusion-forward-reverse.svg)

**Forward** (training only): image → noisier → static, on a fixed schedule. **Reverse** (denoiser training, and generation): static → denoised → image, driven by the learned model. Generation runs the arrow backward, from invented noise, not a real image.

slides.subTitle: Sampling from pure noise
slides.markdown:
To generate a new image, start from a canvas of **pure random noise** and run the learned denoising step repeatedly — each step predicts and removes a bit of noise, and after enough steps (tens to a few thousand, depending on the sampler), what remains is a coherent image that never existed before.

Because the starting noise is random, a different seed gives a different final image from the same model and prompt — that's *why* diffusion is inherently generative: the randomness lives in the starting point, not a decoding choice like an LLM's.

slides.subTitle: Conditioning generation on text
slides.markdown:
Plain diffusion generates *some* realistic image with no control over what it depicts. **Text-to-image** models add conditioning: a text encoder (often built on the same embedding ideas as [Word Embeddings](word-embeddings), scaled up) turns the prompt into a representation the denoising network attends to at every step, steering each noise-removal step toward an image consistent with the description.

This is why prompt wording changes the output so much — the text embedding is literally injected into every step of the reverse process, not just used once at the start.

slides.subTitle: Latent diffusion
slides.markdown:
Running the full noising/denoising process on high-resolution pixels is expensive — every step touches the full pixel grid. **Latent diffusion** (behind Stable Diffusion) compresses the image into a smaller **latent representation** with a separate autoencoder, runs the whole diffusion process there, and decodes back to pixels only once at the end.

This cuts compute dramatically (often 10x+ fewer values per step) with little quality loss, since the latent space still captures the image's visually meaningful structure.

slides.subTitle: Sample quality and diversity vs training stability vs speed
slides.markdown:
| | Diffusion | GANs |
|---|---|---|
| Training stability | Stable — a single well-behaved denoising loss | Notoriously unstable — adversarial game between generator and discriminator |
| Sample diversity | High — covers the data distribution well | Prone to mode collapse — generator narrows to a few outputs |
| Generation speed | Slow — many sequential denoising steps | Fast — a single forward pass |
| Sample quality (current SOTA) | State of the art for images | Was SOTA before diffusion overtook it |

**How to decide:** diffusion is the default choice for state-of-the-art image quality and training reliability today; GANs remain attractive when generation speed (real-time use cases) matters more than the last bit of quality.
